topic: What happens if you fall from a plane without a parachute?
title: Falling Without A Parachute
idea: After about ten seconds you stop speeding up, and the only clues to surviving come from real cases, not tests.
hook: You fall out of a plane with no parachute.

beats.line: You fall faster every second. Guess your top speed.
About ten seconds in, the air pushing up matches gravity.
Belly down, that's about one hundred twenty miles an hour.
Honest truth. Nobody has ever tested how to survive this.
Survivor cases point to three things. None is a guarantee.
Two. Something soft, like snow or trees.
Three. A slope, so the stop takes longer.
Vesna Vulović fell thirty three thousand feet, pinned inside a plane's tail.

end.line: The tail hit a snowy slope. She lived. Two out of three.

description: Fall from a plane with no parachute and you stop speeding up after ten seconds. Then what?

facts.claim: A falling body stops speeding up when air resistance equals weight (terminal velocity). Belly-down (spread-eagle) a skydiver tops out around 55 m/s, about 120 mph (OpenStax: about 200 km/h spread-eagle); it reaches about 90% of that after 8 seconds and 99% after 15, so 'about ten seconds' to stop speeding up.
facts.source: OpenStax University Physics vol. 1 ch. 6.4 https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-1/pages/6-4-drag-force-and-terminal-speed ; Huang, Speed of a skydiver, The Physics Factbook (cited in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminal_velocity)

facts.claim: There is no tested procedure for surviving a fall without a parachute.
Case reports point to landing feet first, on snow, trees or a slope, which spread the stop over more time.
Vesna Vulović survived a fall of 10,160 m (33,333 ft) on 26 January 1972, pinned inside the tail section, which landed on a snowy slope; Guinness record for highest fall survived without a parachute.

factcheck.note: Terminal speed re-checked: OpenStax 6.4 gives about 200 km/h spread-eagle (~124 mph); Physics Factbook (Huang) gives about 55 m/s belly-to-earth (~123 mph), 90% after 8 s, 99% after 15 s. 'About one hundred twenty miles an hour' and 'about ten seconds' fit. On-screen numbers: 120 MPH, 00:10 timer, 33,000 FEET (spoken 'thirty three thousand feet', rounds 33,333 down), 0 tested methods. 'Two out of three' = snow and slope matched her case; not a claim she followed a method.
